lessons.title: Why AI matters — and why you stay in charge
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I use AI, and what do I keep deciding myself?
lessons.blurb: Start from your choices, not the hype. Set one rule you can keep.

resources.label: Elements of AI — free intro course

steps.title: You already know all three of these people
steps.scenario: Look at your group chat. One person runs everything through AI — their work is faster and they're getting way more done. Another swears it off: AI is dangerous, so they do every assignment themselves, by hand. A third uses it for literally everything, no exceptions. They're all talking over each other, and every one of them is sure they're right.
steps.prompt: Before you read on — in one sentence, where do you actually land?

steps.title: Sort these uses
steps.prompt: Which of these keep you learning, and which quietly replace your thinking?

items.text: Ask AI to explain a concept, then re-explain it back in your own words
Paste the homework question and copy the answer
Ask for 3 angles on an essay, then pick and argue one yourself
Let AI write the whole essay and submit it

steps.reveal: The line is not "AI or no AI." It is "did I still do the thinking that matters?"

steps.title: Agency is the real skill
steps.body: AI is useful when a human keeps the goal, the method, and the verification. Speed is not the same as understanding.
steps.mistake: Trusting a fluent answer because it sounds confident.
steps.good: Use AI to improve your reasoning, and skip it when it tempts you to stop thinking.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I am deciding when AI helps me without replacing my thinking. Give me 5 useful use cases and 5 risky shortcuts for someone like me. For each risky shortcut, add one question I should ask myself before using it.
steps.note: Run this in any free AI tool, then keep the 5 risky ones near your desk.

steps.title: Build the stay-in-charge routine
steps.goal: You are stuck on a hard homework problem and want AI help without handing over your thinking.
correct: Try the problem yourself first, even badly
Ask AI to explain only the part you are stuck on
Re-explain the idea back in your own words
Check the answer against your notes or textbook
Write the final answer yourself
steps.note: Notice who starts and who finishes: you do. AI only helps in the middle, and you verify before you trust.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which is the strongest reason to keep a human in charge?

options.text: AI tends to handle the routine stuff fine, so a human mostly needs to step in on the genuinely hard questions
options.feedback: Sounds reasonable, but you often can't tell in advance which question is the hard one. The easy-looking ones are where unverified answers slip past you.

options.text: A fluent answer can still be wrong or low-value
options.feedback: Exactly. Confidence is not proof.

options.text: A lot of teachers and parents are still uncomfortable with AI, so it's safer to keep a person visibly involved for now
options.feedback: That's about how it looks to other people, not about quality. You stay in charge because answers need checking — and that stays true even once everyone is comfortable.

lessons.title: Your first useful AI conversation
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I frame a request so the answer is useful and checkable?
lessons.blurb: A good conversation is a loop, not one-shot magic.

steps.title: Ten minutes, something hard
steps.scenario: You are stuck on photosynthesis with a quiz tomorrow. You want help, but you do not want to just copy and understand nothing.
steps.prompt: What is the first thing you would type?

steps.title: Two ways to ask
steps.strong: You are my tutor. I am studying photosynthesis for a quiz. Ask me one question first, give one hint, then explain simply. Make me try one example before you give the full answer.
steps.why: The strong version sets a role, context, structure, and a required learner check — so the AI coaches instead of dumping an answer.

steps.title: Repair a weak prompt
steps.strong: Goal: understand the water cycle well enough to teach it. Context: I am in 9th grade and confused about condensation vs. evaporation. Constraints: simple words, no jargon without a definition. Format: 4 short steps, then 2 quiz questions for me.

steps.title: Make a loop, not a dump
steps.body: A useful request includes role, context, what help you want, and what the AI should NOT do for you.
steps.mistake: Accepting a full answer immediately, without your own attempt.
steps.good: Ask for a short output first, then a follow-up after you try.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Act like a peer tutor for [your topic]. Ask what I already understand, give one hint, then wait for my attempt. Only after I try, give your fuller explanation.
steps.note: Swap in a topic you actually have due this week.

steps.title: Loop or dump?
steps.prompt: Some requests start a back-and-forth you can check. Others just ask for a finished answer. Sort each one.

items.text: Ask me one question about my topic before you explain anything
Write my lab conclusion for me, full paragraph, ready to turn in
Give me a hint, wait for my attempt, then tell me what I missed
Just explain all of photosynthesis, everything I need for the quiz

steps.reveal: A loop gives you a place to try, fail, and check yourself. A dump skips your attempt — and your attempt is the part that sticks.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What made the strong prompt better?

options.text: It packed in more detail, and adding detail tends to make a prompt work better
options.feedback: Detail only helps when it tells the AI how to help you — a long but vague prompt still fails.

options.text: It gave role, context, and a required check
options.feedback: Yes — structure creates a coaching loop.

options.text: It sounded more serious and academic, which makes the AI take the request seriously
options.feedback: No — it actually asked for simpler words. Tone is not the lever; the structure is.

lessons.title: What AI actually is
lessons.coreQuestion: What is AI really doing, under the confident tone?
lessons.blurb: A pattern system, not a human mind. That frame keeps your options open.

resources.label: Common Sense Media — AI basics

steps.title: "It understands everything"
steps.scenario: A classmate insists the AI "just knows" the answer because it sounds so sure.
steps.prompt: Do you buy it? Why or why not?

steps.title: Which frame holds up?
steps.prompt: Tag each statement as a useful frame or a misconception.

items.text: AI is trained software that generates patterns from data
AI thinks like a human and is almost always right
AI is a perfect, live library lookup
AI is great for fast drafts I then verify

steps.reveal: Patterns are powerful but not infallible. A polished paragraph can still be invented.

steps.title: Generate first, verify always
steps.body: AI is strong at generating language patterns fast. That gives you drafts and ideas quickly.
steps.mistake: Confusing fluency with truth.
steps.good: Use AI for options, then test each against your own understanding and a source.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Explain what AI is to a 14-year-old in 3 plain lines, without saying it is "smart like a person." Then give me 2 trap questions I can use to check whether a definition is too naive.
steps.note: Use the trap questions on a friend — or on yourself.

steps.title: Spot the mind-words
steps.passage: This chatbot truly understands you. It knows every fact, thinks like a genius, and never gets things wrong — so you can stop checking its answers.
steps.reveal: Every word you clicked treats software like a person. Swap them for "generates likely text" and suddenly the claim sounds a lot less safe to trust.

fields.placeholder: AI just knows the answer

fields.label: Reality
fields.placeholder: AI generates likely patterns

fields.label: So I will verify…
fields.placeholder: any fact I would repeat out loud

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Best one-line definition?

options.text: Software that recognizes and generates patterns from data
options.feedback: Practical and honest.

options.text: A digital mind that genuinely understands you once it has seen enough about a topic
options.feedback: Fluency is not understanding — treating it like a mind makes you trust it too much.

options.text: A smarter kind of search engine that pulls answers from a mostly reliable index of the web
options.feedback: It generates text rather than looking things up, so it can invent things no source ever said.

lessons.title: What an LLM is, without the magic
lessons.coreQuestion: Why is it so fluent, and why can it still be confidently wrong?
lessons.blurb: Tokens, context, and likely next words become your control points.

steps.title: Fluent, and still wrong
steps.scenario: Your model writes a smooth paragraph but skips one requirement you clearly stated.
steps.prompt: What do you think happened inside?

steps.title: Predict the next word
steps.note: An LLM picks likely next tokens from context. Fluency comes from "what usually follows," not from looking anything up.

steps.title: Context is the steering wheel
steps.body: An LLM predicts likely next tokens given your context and its training. If a key constraint is missing or buried, output drifts — confidently.
steps.mistake: Assuming it "remembers" everything like a person.
steps.good: State constraints explicitly, set an output format, and ask for a self-check.

steps.title: Where it goes wrong
steps.weak: Write about the French Revolution. (then later) Also keep it under 100 words.
steps.strong: In under 100 words, write about the French Revolution for a 9th grader. End by listing the 2 facts I should double-check.
steps.why: Front-loading the constraint and asking for a verification list fights the "drift" you just saw.

steps.title: Repair the prompt so context stays visible
steps.strong: Explain photosynthesis to someone like me in under 120 words. Use one concrete analogy, define glucose, and end with 2 facts I should verify in a biology source.

steps.title: How it works vs. how it feels
steps.prompt: Tag each claim: is this actually how an LLM works, or just how it feels when you use it?
buckets: How it feels, not how it works

items.text: It picks likely next tokens based on your context and its training
It looks up every fact in a live database before answering
A constraint buried late in the chat can fade, so output drifts
If the answer sounds confident, it must have checked it somewhere

steps.reveal: Likelihood is not lookup. The confident tone comes from fluent prediction, not from verification — that part stays your job.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Give me one 2-minute exercise that teaches a friend the difference between fluency and truth, using a single AI answer as the example.
steps.note: Bonus: run the exercise and see if they get fooled.

fields.label: I will keep context visible by...
fields.placeholder: putting the goal and audience first

fields.label: I will prevent drift by...
fields.placeholder: setting length, format, and must-include details

fields.label: I will check truth by...
fields.placeholder: asking what to verify outside the model

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Why can an LLM be fluent but wrong?

options.text: It predicts likely text, which is not the same as verified fact
options.feedback: Right — likelihood ≠ truth.

options.text: Its training data probably contained mistakes, so those wrong facts leak into its answers
options.feedback: Training data does have errors, but that is not the core reason — even a model trained on clean text can drift, because it is generating likely words, not checking facts.

options.text: It mostly knows the truth, but it loses track of long prompts and fills gaps from memory
options.feedback: Context limits are real, but the deeper issue is that it never "knows" truth at all — it predicts what text usually comes next, which can sound right and still be wrong.

lessons.title: Prompt repair: goal, context, constraints, format
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a weak ask into a useful instruction?
lessons.blurb: The difference between asking and prompting — a repeatable repair.

resources.label: Stanford CRAFT — AI literacy resources

steps.title: Boring answer again
steps.scenario: Same question, but the answer comes back generic and useless. The question was not the problem — the prompt was.
steps.prompt: What is one thing you would add to fix it?

steps.title: Repair it live
steps.strong: Goal: a study summary I can revise from tonight. Context: 10th-grade biology, cell division, quiz Friday. Constraints: no homework answers given away; define any term you use. Format: 3 key ideas, 1 common mistake, and a 2-question self-quiz.

steps.title: Prompts are instructions
steps.body: A prompt is executable instruction, not a wish. Better structure → more control.
steps.mistake: A polished sentence with an unclear goal still fails.
steps.good: Keep the goal concrete, constraints explicit, and ask for a quick self-check from the AI.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is my prompt: "[paste your weak prompt]". Rewrite it using Goal, Context, Constraints, Format. Then show me the improved answer and tell me which change mattered most.
steps.note: Compare the before/after - keep the diff in your Saved Notes if it helps.

steps.title: Control or decoration?
steps.prompt: You are repairing a vague prompt by adding pieces to it. Sort each addition: does it actually steer the answer, or just pad the sentence?

items.text: "For my 10th-grade biology class, quiz is Friday"
"Please make it really good and high quality"
"Do not give away answers — define every term you use"
"If you can, whenever you get a chance, thanks!"
"Format: 3 key ideas, then a 2-question self-quiz"

steps.reveal: Goal, context, constraints, and format are things the model can act on. "Good" and "please" are not — control comes from specifics, not politeness.

steps.question: Which piece most often fixes a vague prompt first?

options.text: A concrete goal
options.feedback: Usually yes — without it, everything else floats.

options.text: More polite wording
options.feedback: Politeness does not add control.

options.text: Making it longer
options.feedback: Length without structure does not help.

lessons.title: Data, training & patterns
lessons.coreQuestion: Where does an AI’s “knowledge” come from?
lessons.blurb: Training turns examples into patterns. Useful, but not the same as knowing.

resources.label: Elements of AI — machine learning basics

steps.title: It feels like it just knows
steps.scenario: You ask an AI for a study plan, a poem, and a history summary. It answers all three like it has seen the inside of every classroom.
steps.prompt: Where do you think that ability came from?

steps.title: Training source or live fact?
steps.prompt: Sort what comes from training patterns versus what would need a current source or tool.

items.text: Writing a sentence that sounds like a lab report
Knowing whether your school canceled practice today
Recognizing that "photosynthesis" belongs with plants and light
Checking the exact deadline on your teacher’s website

steps.reveal: Training gives the model patterns. Current facts need a current source, a tool, or your own check.

steps.title: Patterns become predictions
steps.stem: In a recipe, after "preheat the oven to" you often see
steps.note: The model is not opening a cookbook. It has learned which kinds of text usually follow other text.

steps.title: Training is pattern learning
steps.body: AI systems are trained on lots of examples so they can predict, classify, or generate new outputs that match patterns in those examples.
steps.mistake: Treating training data like a perfect memory bank or a live database.
steps.good: Use AI for pattern-heavy work, then verify any fact, quote, date, rule, or local detail.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Explain training data to me using one school analogy and one sports or arts analogy. Then list 5 things a trained model can do well and 5 things I should verify somewhere else.
steps.note: Keep the verify list. It is the practical part.

steps.title: Spot the overclaims
steps.passage: Once a model is trained, it knows the facts in its data, remembers them perfectly, and always gives accurate answers, so double-checking is unnecessary.
steps.reveal: Those words treat training like a flawless memory bank. Training learns patterns from examples, so the output sounds right — but any fact, date, or rule still needs a check.

fields.placeholder: examples, drafts, explanations

fields.label: I will verify facts like...
fields.placeholder: dates, quotes, current rules

fields.label: My first source check will be...
fields.placeholder: teacher page / official site / textbook

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest way to describe training?

options.text: The model stores most of what it read during training, so if a fact appeared in the data you can usually trust it to recall that fact correctly
options.feedback: Tempting, but no. Training compresses examples into patterns, not a stored archive of facts, so even things it "read" can come out wrong.

options.text: The model learns patterns from examples, then generates from those patterns
options.feedback: Exactly. That is useful, but it still needs verification.

options.text: The model mostly works by looking things up as it goes, pulling from the web or a database whenever it needs a fact to answer
options.feedback: Not by default. Some AI tools bolt search on top, but the model itself generates from what it learned in training.

lessons.title: Context windows & memory
lessons.coreQuestion: What does the AI actually remember, and for how long?
lessons.blurb: The model responds to what is in the current context. Memory is not magic.

steps.title: "But I already told it"
steps.scenario: You told an AI your project rules at the start. Ten messages later, it ignores one and gives advice that breaks the assignment.
steps.prompt: Did it forget, miss the rule, or never really remember like a person?

steps.title: In context or out of reach?
steps.prompt: Sort what the AI can use right now versus what you need to restate or provide again.

items.text: A rubric you pasted two messages ago
A file you never uploaded or pasted
A constraint buried 40 messages back in a long chat
The format you put in the prompt it is answering now

steps.reveal: If it matters, keep it visible. Important instructions belong near the task, not buried.

steps.title: Move the rule into view
steps.weak: Make this better but remember my teacher’s rules from before.
steps.strong: Goal: improve my paragraph without changing my argument. Context: 10th-grade English, persuasive paragraph. Constraints: keep my voice, do not add outside facts, and follow this rubric: [paste rubric]. Format: return a revised paragraph plus 3 notes explaining what changed.

steps.title: Context is working memory
steps.body: A context window is the information the model can use for the current response. Some products add saved memory, but you should not assume it has the exact thing you meant.
steps.mistake: Saying "you know what I mean" when the instruction is not visible.
steps.good: Restate the goal, paste key constraints, and ask the AI to repeat the rules before it works.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Before helping me, summarize the constraints I gave you in 3 bullets. If any constraint is missing or unclear, ask me a question instead of guessing. Then complete the task.
steps.note: This works especially well when a rubric or teacher rule matters.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What should you do when a rule really matters?

options.text: Trust that it remembers, since most chats are short enough that nothing gets lost
options.feedback: It often works in short chats, but you cannot tell from the outside when earlier context gets missed or compressed. For rules that matter, do not rely on it.

options.text: Put the rule close to the task and ask the AI to confirm it
options.feedback: Right. Keep important context visible.

options.text: State the rule once near the start, since repeating it later might just clutter the conversation
options.feedback: Restating a rule near the task does not clutter anything — it helps. Instructions far from the current task are exactly the ones that get missed.

lessons.title: Why AI hallucinates
lessons.coreQuestion: Why does it invent things — and how do I catch it?
lessons.blurb: A confident answer can be a guess wearing a suit. Learn the catch routine.

resources.label: Common Sense Media — AI and misinformation

steps.title: The fake quote problem
steps.scenario: An AI gives you a perfect-looking quote for an essay. The wording is strong, the author sounds right, and the citation looks real.
steps.prompt: What would you check before using it?

steps.title: Safe to use or verify first?
steps.prompt: Sort each AI output by what you should do next.

items.text: Three possible titles for your presentation
A quote supposedly from a scientist
A made-up practice problem for algebra
A statistic about teen phone use in 2026

steps.reveal: Ideas can be useful without being true. Claims need proof.

steps.title: Run a hallucination check
steps.claim: A famous researcher said, "AI literacy is the new oxygen of education."
steps: Copy the exact quote into a search engine with quotation marks.
Search the person’s official page or a reliable publication, not only random quote sites.
If you cannot find the quote in a trustworthy place, do not use it as real.
Ask the AI for a safer replacement: "Give me a paraphrase I can verify, not a quote."
steps.note: The goal is not to prove the AI wrong. The goal is to avoid repeating something you cannot stand behind.

steps.title: Hallucination is not drama
steps.body: A hallucination is when an AI generates something false or unsupported as if it were true. It happens because the system is generating likely text, not proving each claim.
steps.mistake: Thinking a citation, title, or quote is real because it is formatted correctly.
steps.good: Ask for uncertainty, sources you can open, and a verification plan before using claims.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is a claim I might use: "[paste claim]". Treat it as unverified. Give me a 4-step plan to check it, tell me what source type would count as strong evidence, and rewrite it in safer language if I cannot verify it.
steps.note: Use this on one claim from homework, a video, or a post.

steps.title: Build the catch routine
steps.goal: Use facts from an AI answer in your essay without repeating something false.
correct: Pick out the checkable claims: quotes, stats, names, dates
Search each claim in a source you could show a teacher
Keep what you verified; cut or soften what you could not
Cite the real source you found, not the AI
steps.note: Same order every time: find the claims, find the sources, then decide what survives. The AI is never the citation.
