steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which output is most dangerous to trust without checking?

options.text: A list of brainstormed club names, since one of them could already belong to another group
options.feedback: Low risk. A taken name is annoying, but you would find out fast — truth is not really the issue with brainstorms.

options.text: A specific quote with a polished citation
options.feedback: Yes. Formatting can look real even when the source is invented.

options.text: A silly analogy for photosynthesis, because a weak analogy might quietly teach the wrong idea
options.feedback: An analogy can mislead a little, but you treat it as a rough teaching aid — you are not repeating it as a fact.

lessons.title: Models, tools & agents
lessons.coreQuestion: What is the difference between a model, a tool, and an agent?
lessons.blurb: Separate the brain, the instruments, and the doer before you trust the system.

steps.title: One AI, three different jobs
steps.scenario: An app answers your question, searches the web, and adds a calendar reminder. People call all of it "AI," but those are not the same job.
steps.prompt: Which part is generating, which part is using a tool, and which part is acting for you?

steps.title: Name the part
steps.prompt: Sort each description into the closest bucket.

items.text: Generates a draft email from your instructions
Opens a calculator to solve a precise equation
Searches a website for current ticket prices
Predicts likely next words in a paragraph

steps.reveal: The model generates. Tools fetch or do specific things. Agents combine steps toward a goal.

steps.title: Pick tools for a safe agent
steps.goal: Help plan a study session by checking a calendar, finding open time, and drafting a study checklist.
steps.note: Give an agent only the tools it needs for the job. Extra power is extra risk.

steps.title: Capability comes in layers
steps.body: A model can generate text. A tool can retrieve, calculate, send, edit, or store. An agent uses a model plus tools to pursue a goal through multiple steps.
steps.mistake: Trusting a system more just because it can act in the world.
steps.good: Check the goal, permissions, tools, and stop conditions before letting anything act for you.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: For this task: "[paste a task]", split the AI system into model, tools, and agent behavior. Tell me what permissions are necessary, what permissions would be risky, and where a human should approve before action.
steps.note: Try it with a real task like planning, email, research, or reminders.

fields.label: Agent goal
fields.placeholder: what it should accomplish

fields.label: Allowed tools
fields.placeholder: only what it needs

fields.label: Human approval required before...
fields.placeholder: sending, buying, deleting, posting

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What makes an agent different from a plain model response?

options.text: It usually runs on a bigger, more capable model than a normal chat reply
options.feedback: Not quite. An agent can run on the same model. What changes is that it can act, not how smart it is.

options.text: It can use tools and take steps toward a goal
options.feedback: Right. That is why permissions and approval matter.

options.text: Once it has been tested, it can mostly handle tasks without someone checking its work
options.feedback: Careful. The more a system acts in the world, the more its actions need review, not less.

lessons.title: Better follow-ups
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I steer a conversation instead of restarting it?
lessons.blurb: Good AI work is usually not one perfect prompt. It is steering, checking, and narrowing.

steps.title: The answer is almost useful
steps.scenario: You ask AI for help and the answer is not bad, but it is too broad, misses your situation, and gives advice you already knew.
steps.prompt: Do you start over, or do you steer it?

steps.title: Restart or follow up?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it throws away context or improves the current conversation.

items.text: “Never mind. Give me a better answer.”
“Use the same plan, but make it fit a 20-minute study session.”
“That is too generic. Ask me 3 questions before revising.”
Opening a new chat every time the first answer is imperfect

steps.reveal: A follow-up keeps useful context and adds direction. Restarting often loses what the model already learned about the task.

steps.title: Turn frustration into steering
steps.weak: That answer is bad. Try again.
steps.strong: Keep the 3-part structure, but make it specific to someone studying after school for 25 minutes. Add one example for each part, and end by asking me what constraint you may have missed.

steps.title: Conversation is control
steps.body: A good AI conversation is a loop: ask, inspect, steer, verify, then use. Follow-ups are how you turn a generic answer into something that fits.
steps.mistake: Treating the first answer as the final answer.
steps.good: Name what to keep, what to change, what to add, and what to check.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is an AI answer I almost like: [paste answer]. Help me improve it with 4 follow-ups: one to narrow it, one to make it more concrete, one to check assumptions, and one to make the final output easier to use.
steps.note: This works best when the first answer is close, not useless.

fields.label: Keep
fields.placeholder: what was useful in the first answer

fields.label: Change
fields.placeholder: what needs to be different

fields.label: Add
fields.placeholder: missing context, example, or constraint

fields.label: Check
fields.placeholder: assumption or fact to verify

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which follow-up gives you the most control?

options.text: “This is close to what I wanted, so go ahead and improve it however you think makes the most sense for my situation.”
options.feedback: It sounds specific, but every decision is handed back to the model. Without saying what to keep or change, you can't predict what comes back.

options.text: “Keep the structure, make it fit my 20-minute limit, and ask one question if a constraint is missing.”
options.feedback: Right. It says what to keep, change, and check.

options.text: “Honestly, it might be easier to scrap this draft and try a totally different approach — a fresh start could land closer to what I'm picturing.”
options.feedback: Starting over can occasionally help, but it throws away the context you already built up, and the model still doesn't know what 'closer' means.

lessons.title: Roles, formats & constraints
lessons.coreQuestion: How do roles and formats change what I get back?
lessons.blurb: Role, format, and constraints are control knobs. Use them deliberately.

steps.title: Same topic, different answer
steps.scenario: Ask for “help with my presentation” and you get generic advice. Ask for a skeptical reviewer, a slide outline, and a 5-minute limit, and the answer changes completely.
steps.prompt: Which part changed the answer most: role, format, or constraint?

steps.title: Name the control knob
steps.prompt: Sort each prompt part by what it controls.

items.text: Act as a skeptical science fair judge
Return a 6-slide outline
Use no more than 120 words
Be a patient tutor who asks before explaining

steps.reveal: Role changes the lens. Format changes the shape. Constraints set boundaries.

steps.title: Add the missing controls
steps.weak: Help me with my history project.
steps.strong: Act as a history project coach. Format: give me a 5-part outline with one question under each part. Constraints: do not write the final paragraphs, keep it at 9th-grade level, and flag any claim that needs a source. Success check: end with what I should do next myself.

steps.title: Roles are not costumes
steps.body: A role is useful when it changes what the model pays attention to: tutor, reviewer, planner, debate opponent, editor. A format is useful when it makes the output easier to inspect.
steps.mistake: Adding a fancy role but no task, no constraints, and no check.
steps.good: Use role + task + format + constraints + success check.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Take this task: [paste task]. Give me 3 prompt versions using different roles: tutor, critic, and project manager. For each, choose a format and one constraint that would make the answer easier to use.
steps.note: Compare the answers. The best role depends on the job.

fields.label: Role
fields.placeholder: tutor / critic / planner / editor

fields.label: Format
fields.placeholder: table, checklist, outline, questions

fields.label: Constraint
fields.placeholder: time, level, sources, length

fields.label: Success check
fields.placeholder: how I know the answer is useful

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest prompt pattern?

options.text: Pick a strong role first, since a good persona tends to handle format and constraints on its own
options.feedback: A role changes the lens, but it does not set the task, the shape of the output, or how you will check the answer.

options.text: Role + task + format + constraints + success check
options.feedback: Yes. That combination gives both direction and review.

options.text: Keep the prompt short and open-ended so the model has room to find the best approach itself
options.feedback: Open-ended can work for brainstorming, but for real tasks you lose the structure that makes answers easy to inspect.

lessons.title: Getting AI to teach you
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I make AI a tutor, not an answer vending machine?
lessons.blurb: A tutor makes you think. An answer machine lets you skip the work.

steps.title: The homework shortcut trap
steps.scenario: You ask AI for the answer, understand it for two seconds, then cannot solve the next problem alone.
steps.prompt: What would a good tutor do differently?

steps.title: Tutor move or answer-machine move?
steps.prompt: Sort the AI behaviors by whether they protect your learning.

items.text: Ask what I already tried before explaining
Give the final answer immediately
Give one hint, then wait for my attempt
Write the whole assignment in my voice

steps.reveal: A tutor creates effort at the right moment. Too much help can feel good and still weaken learning.

steps.title: Repair the tutor prompt
steps.strong: Act as a tutor. Do not give the final answer first. Ask me what I tried, give one hint at a time, wait for my attempt, then check my reasoning and give a similar practice problem.

steps.title: Learning needs friction
steps.body: The best AI tutor does not remove all struggle. It adjusts the struggle: hints before answers, questions before lectures, practice before confidence.
steps.mistake: Confusing “I read the answer” with “I can do it myself.”
steps.good: Ask AI to question, hint, test, and correct you without taking over.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Teach me [topic]. Start by asking what I already know. Give me one hint at a time, do not reveal the full answer until I try, and end with a short quiz plus one transfer problem.
steps.note: Use this when the goal is learning, not just finishing.

fields.label: Topic I am learning
fields.placeholder: algebra, photosynthesis, essay thesis

fields.label: Do not...
fields.placeholder: give the final answer first

fields.label: Do...
fields.placeholder: ask, hint, check, quiz

fields.label: Proof I learned it
fields.placeholder: I can solve a similar problem alone

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which request turns AI into a better tutor?

options.text: “Walk me through the full solution step by step, since seeing a complete worked example is usually how I learn best.”
options.feedback: Worked examples can help, but if you watch the whole solution before trying, you can follow every step and still freeze on the next problem. Attempt first, then compare.

options.text: “Give one hint, wait for my attempt, then check my reasoning.”
options.feedback: Right. That keeps you doing the important thinking.

options.text: “Just give me the answer this once — I'm short on time tonight and I'll go back and study the method later.”
options.feedback: This feels reasonable in the moment, but 'later' rarely happens, and you skip the struggle that builds the skill. The task gets done; the learning does not.

lessons.title: Human agency
lessons.coreQuestion: Where must a human stay in the loop?
lessons.blurb: Use AI for help, but keep the goal, values, and final decision human.

steps.title: The AI sounds sure
steps.scenario: An AI recommends which club you should quit, which class you should take, and how to apologize to a friend. The advice sounds calm and reasonable.
steps.prompt: Which part can AI help with, and which part should stay yours?

steps.title: AI helper or human decision?
steps.prompt: Sort each task by whether AI can help or whether the human must own the final decision.

items.text: List possible tradeoffs before choosing a class
Decide what matters most to your family or values
Draft three respectful ways to start a hard conversation
Choose whether to forgive someone

steps.reveal: AI can widen your thinking. It should not replace your responsibility for values, relationships, and consequences.

steps.title: Put the human back in charge
steps.weak: Tell me what I should do.
steps.strong: Help me think through this decision without deciding for me. Decision: [describe]. Options: [list]. Values I care about: [list]. Give tradeoffs, questions I should ask, and what information is missing. Do not tell me the final choice.

steps.title: Agency is not anti-AI
steps.body: Human agency means you use AI as a thinking aid while keeping ownership of goals, values, consent, and final action. The safer pattern is: AI suggests, human judges.
steps.mistake: Treating confident advice as permission to stop deciding.
steps.good: Ask for options, consequences, missing information, and counterarguments before you choose.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I have a decision: [describe]. Do not decide for me. Give me 3 options, tradeoffs for each, what information is missing, and 5 questions that help me make the decision myself.
steps.note: Use this for low-risk decisions first, then notice how much better the conversation gets.

fields.label: AI can help me...
fields.placeholder: list options, questions, tradeoffs

fields.label: I must own...
fields.placeholder: values, relationships, final action

fields.label: Before acting, I will...
fields.placeholder: pause, check, ask a person, decide myself

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which use keeps human agency strongest?

options.text: Go with the AI's recommendation when you feel stuck, since it has seen far more situations like yours than you have
options.feedback: Feeling stuck is exactly when the choice matters most. Seeing lots of patterns is not the same as knowing your values — the judgment is still yours.

options.text: Ask AI for options, tradeoffs, and missing information, then decide yourself
options.feedback: Right. AI supports the thinking, not the ownership.

options.text: Make the call yourself first, but switch to the AI's answer whenever it disagrees, because it probably caught something you missed
options.feedback: Disagreement is a reason to ask more questions, not to hand over the decision. You can take the new information and still decide yourself.

steps.title: The link works. Now what?
steps.scenario: You ask AI for evidence and it cites a real article. You click it and it opens — a blog post from 2014 about an early version of the app you are writing about, and most of it is copied from the company's own press release. Nothing is fake. But is it actually evidence?
steps.prompt: What about this source would make you hesitate, even though it exists?

steps.title: Real, but is it strong?
steps.prompt: Every one of these sources is real and opens fine. Sort them by whether they could carry a claim in your essay.

items.text: A decade-old blog post about an older version of the product
A recent study that measured the exact thing you are claiming
A news article that mentions your topic but not your statistic
A government dataset updated this year, covering your question
A site that reworded a company press release without checking it

steps.reveal: Existing is the lowest bar a source can clear. Strong means current enough, independent, and about your exact claim.

steps.title: Build a lateral-reading routine
steps.goal: Decide whether a real source is strong enough to cite, in about three minutes.
correct: Open the source and skim what it actually says
Check the date and who published it
Search what other sites say about that publisher
Confirm it supports your exact sentence, not just the topic
Shrink or revise the claim if the evidence is narrower
choices: Open the source and skim what it actually says
Check the date and who published it
Search what other sites say about that publisher
Confirm it supports your exact sentence, not just the topic
Shrink or revise the claim if the evidence is narrower
steps.note: Step three is lateral reading: leaving the page to see what others say about it. Fact-checkers do this instead of judging a site by its own design and About page.

steps.title: A real source can still fail you
steps.body: A source can let you down in quieter ways than being fake: it can be too old, about something slightly different, or just an echo of a press release with no independent checking. Citing it is technically honest and still misleading.
steps.mistake: Stopping the check the moment the link opens. "It exists" feels like verification, but it only rules out one failure.
steps.good: Grade the source on four things: date, independence, who is behind it, and whether it covers your exact sentence. If it fails one, find a better source or soften the claim.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I am thinking of citing this source for the claim "[paste your claim]": [paste the link or describe the source]. Do not tell me whether the claim is true. Instead, list the questions I should answer about this source's date, its author or publisher, whether it is original reporting or secondhand, and whether it covers my exact claim. Then suggest what a stronger source type would look like.
steps.note: Use this on a source you were already planning to cite. The interesting cases are the ones that look fine.

fields.label: Source I am grading
fields.placeholder: title or link of the real source

fields.label: Date and independence
fields.placeholder: how old is it, and is it original or an echo?

fields.label: Does it cover my exact sentence?
fields.placeholder: same claim, or just the same topic?

fields.label: Verdict
fields.placeholder: cite it, replace it, or shrink my claim

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: A citation from AI turns out to be real, and the page opens fine. What still has to be true before you cite it?

options.text: It should appear on the first page of search results
options.feedback: Ranking measures popularity and search habits, not reliability. Weak sources rank well all the time.

options.text: It actually backs the exact sentence you wrote
options.feedback: Right. Date, independence, and fit to your exact claim are what make a real source usable — existing is just the first hurdle.

options.text: It should come from a site with a professional design and a detailed About page
options.feedback: Design is cheap and the About page is written by the site itself. Read laterally — see what other sources say about the publisher.

lessons.title: Verification & sources
lessons.coreQuestion: The citation is real — but is it strong enough to use?
lessons.blurb: Most weak sources are not fake. They are old, off-topic, or echoes. Learn to grade them.

resources.label: Stanford Civic Online Reasoning — lateral reading
SIFT: the four moves (Mike Caulfield)

lessons.title: Bias, fairness & perspective
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I spot bias in an AI answer?
lessons.blurb: Bias often hides in loaded words, missing groups, and one-sided framing.

steps.title: The answer sounds neutral
steps.scenario: AI summarizes a debate and says one side is “reasonable” while the other is “emotional.” It never explains why.
steps.prompt: What words or missing perspectives would you inspect first?

steps.title: Bias signal or fair move?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it helps fairness or signals possible bias.

items.text: Using loaded labels without evidence
Naming what evidence would change the answer
Ignoring the group most affected by the decision
Showing the strongest argument from more than one side

steps.reveal: Fairness starts with noticing framing: who is named, who is missing, and which words carry judgment.

steps.title: Spot the loaded language
steps.passage: The responsible students wanted reasonable AI rules, but the lazy students complained because restrictions would expose their shortcuts.
steps.reveal: You caught the framing words. They push you toward a judgment before evidence appears.

steps.title: Bias is not only being mean
steps.body: Bias can be obvious, but it can also be a missing perspective, a loaded comparison, a hidden assumption, or a pattern copied from flawed data.
steps.mistake: Calling an answer fair just because it sounds calm.
steps.good: Ask who is missing, what assumptions are being made, and how the answer changes under another perspective.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Review this AI answer for bias: [paste answer]. Look for loaded words, missing perspectives, hidden assumptions, and what evidence would make the answer fairer. Then rewrite it more neutrally.
steps.note: This is useful for summaries, debates, policies, and recommendations.

fields.label: Loaded words to inspect
fields.placeholder: lazy, normal, extreme, obvious

fields.label: Missing perspective
fields.placeholder: who is affected but not represented

fields.label: Neutral rewrite move
fields.placeholder: separate evidence from judgment

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which is the best first bias check?

options.text: Check whether the answer keeps a calm, even-handed tone, since biased writing tends to sound heated or one-sided
options.feedback: Tone is easy to fake. A calm, polite answer can still carry loaded framing — check the actual words, not the mood.

options.text: Look for loaded words, missing perspectives, and hidden assumptions
options.feedback: Right. Those are practical things you can inspect.

options.text: Compare the answer against your own view, since bias mostly shows up where it disagrees with you
options.feedback: Your own view can be biased too. Disagreement is not proof of bias — inspect the framing itself: who is named, who is missing, which words judge.

lessons.title: Privacy & personal data
lessons.coreQuestion: What should I never paste into an AI tool?
lessons.blurb: Good AI habits include knowing what not to share.

steps.title: The convenient paste
steps.scenario: You want AI to rewrite an email, so you paste the whole thread. It includes names, phone numbers, a private problem, and a school account detail.
steps.prompt: Which parts should have been removed first?

steps.title: Paste or protect?
steps.prompt: Sort what is usually safer to share versus what should be removed or anonymized.

items.text: A made-up example sentence
Someone’s full name plus private situation
A general task description with no identifying details
Passwords, tokens, addresses, or private account details

steps.reveal: The safest prompt often uses a fake example, initials, or a summary instead of raw private data.

steps.title: Anonymize the request
steps.weak: Rewrite this message from Maya to Mr. Chen about her medical appointment: [private thread].
steps.strong: Rewrite a short message from a student to a teacher asking to reschedule because of a private appointment. Do not include names, medical details, addresses, or account information. Tone: respectful and brief.

steps.title: Privacy is part of skill
steps.body: Before using AI, decide what data the tool does not need. Names, locations, passwords, health details, private conflicts, and account information usually do not belong in prompts.
steps.mistake: Thinking “I am only asking for wording” means private context is safe to paste.
steps.good: Summarize, anonymize, or use a fake example when the exact private details are not needed.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Help me rewrite this request without using private details. First ask me what information can be anonymized. Then create a safe version of the prompt before answering.
steps.note: Do this before pasting messages, documents, screenshots, or personal stories.

fields.label: Never paste
fields.placeholder: passwords, addresses, private names...

fields.label: Replace with
fields.placeholder: initials, fake example, summary

fields.label: Before sending, I will check for...
fields.placeholder: identifying details or secrets

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest way to ask AI for help with a private message?

options.text: Paste the whole thread, since the AI usually writes a better reply when it can see the full context of the conversation
options.feedback: Context helps, but the AI rarely needs the private details to fix wording. A short summary gives it enough.

options.text: Summarize the situation and remove names, secrets, and identifying details
options.feedback: Right. Give only what the task needs.

options.text: Paste it as written, but tell the AI up front not to store or remember anything from the message
options.feedback: By then the data has already left your hands. Protect it before sending, not after.

lessons.title: When not to use AI
lessons.coreQuestion: When is the right move to NOT use AI?
lessons.blurb: Sometimes the strongest AI skill is choosing a human, a source, or your own effort.

steps.title: The fastest tool is not always the right tool
steps.scenario: You can use AI to reply to a friend, solve a practice problem, summarize a sensitive story, or make a medical guess. Fast does not mean wise.
steps.prompt: Which one would you avoid first, and why?

steps.title: Use AI or pause?
steps.prompt: Sort the situations by whether AI can help or whether you should pause and use another route.

items.text: Brainstorming possible titles for a club poster
Entering someone’s private story with names and identifying details
Getting hints on a practice problem without final answers
Making a medical, legal, or safety decision from AI alone

steps.reveal: AI is strongest when the risk is low, the human stays in charge, and you can verify. Pause when privacy, safety, law, health, or relationships are at stake.

steps.title: Build the pause routine
steps.goal: Decide whether to use AI on a sensitive task.
correct: Name the risk
Remove private details if AI is still useful
Choose a trusted source or person when stakes are high
Use AI only for low-risk framing or questions
Make the final decision yourself
steps.note: The pause routine keeps speed from overriding judgment.

steps.title: Not using AI is not falling behind
steps.body: The goal is not to use AI everywhere. The goal is to know when it helps, when it weakens learning, and when another source or person is safer.
steps.mistake: Using AI because it is available, not because it fits the risk.
steps.good: Ask: What is the cost of being wrong, what data would I expose, and who should decide?

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: For this task: [paste task]. Help me decide whether to use AI. Rate the privacy risk, learning risk, accuracy risk, and human-relationship risk. If I should not use AI, suggest a safer next step.
steps.note: This makes AI help with the decision about AI, while you still choose.

fields.label: Risk that makes me pause
fields.placeholder: privacy, safety, learning, relationship

fields.label: Better next step
fields.placeholder: ask teacher, check source, try myself

fields.label: If I use AI, only for...
fields.placeholder: questions, outline, low-risk wording

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: When should you avoid relying on AI alone?

options.text: When the stakes involve health, safety, law, privacy, or a relationship
options.feedback: Right. Use a trusted source, person, or your own judgment.

options.text: When you need ideas, since even a casual brainstorm list usually turns out better if a person writes it without AI
options.feedback: Low-risk brainstorming is actually one of the safer uses — a bad idea on a list costs you almost nothing, and you still pick the final one.

options.text: Mostly when the model sounds unsure of itself; if it answers confidently, it has probably checked itself and you can lean on it
options.feedback: Confidence is part of the writing style, not a sign of accuracy. You have to judge the risk yourself instead of waiting for the model to flag it.

lessons.title: Studying & school
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to actually be ready on test day?
lessons.blurb: Rereading feels like studying. Testing yourself is studying. AI is good at making the second one easy — quizzes and flashcards built from your own notes, spaced out before the exam.

resources.label: The Learning Scientists: Six strategies for effective learning (free downloads)
Retrieval Practice: research on testing yourself to learn

steps.title: You knew it until the test started
steps.scenario: You spent the whole weekend on the history chapter. Read it twice, highlighted half of it, watched a review video. By Sunday night everything felt familiar — you would have bet money you knew it. Monday the test says: explain the three causes from memory. The page in your head is yellow and blurry, and the familiar feeling turns out to be the only thing you memorized.
steps.prompt: The chapter felt easy because you were looking at it. What changed when you had to produce it with the book closed?

steps.title: Feels like studying vs. is studying
steps.prompt: The dividing line: does your brain have to pull the answer out of memory, or just recognize it on the page? Sort each move.

items.text: Rereading the chapter a third time
Covering your notes and writing down what you remember
Highlighting most of the page in yellow
Having AI turn your notes into flashcards, then answering each one before flipping it
Watching the explainer video again because it made sense last time
Taking a practice test cold, then grading it to find weak spots

steps.reveal: Recognizing is not recalling. Rereading and highlighting make material feel familiar — researchers call it the illusion of fluency. The exam tests retrieval, so practice retrieval.

steps.title: The illusion of fluency
steps.body: When you reread something, it gets smoother and more familiar each pass — and your brain reads that smoothness as knowing. It is not. On test day the page is gone and only what you can retrieve is left. Decades of memory research point the same way: testing yourself strengthens memory more than restudying, and spreading that testing over several days beats one long cram. This is where AI is genuinely useful — not for answers, but for turning your own notes into an endless supply of practice questions, fresh ones each round, with the answers held back until you try.
steps.mistake: Judging how ready you are by how familiar the material feels while you are looking at it.
steps.good: Judge readiness by what you can produce with the notes closed. Quiz scores from memory are the honest signal; the familiar feeling is not.

steps.title: Build the exam-prep loop
steps.goal: A test in five days. Turn your notes into spaced self-testing instead of one rereading marathon.
correct: Gather your own class notes for the unit
Have AI write quiz questions from those notes, answers hidden
Answer each question from memory, in writing
Grade it and flag every question you missed
Two days later, re-test the flagged ones plus a few new questions
steps.note: Notice what AI does in this loop: it writes the questions and hides the answers. Your brain does the retrieving — that part is not outsourceable.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here are my notes for [class/unit]: [paste your notes]. Make a 10-question quiz from these notes only — mix straight recall with a few 'explain why' questions. Show one question at a time and do not reveal any answer until I have typed my attempt. At the end, list the questions I missed and tell me to re-test those in two days.
steps.note: Using your own notes matters twice: the quiz matches what your class actually covered, and any gaps in the notes show up now instead of on the test.

fields.label: Test and date
fields.placeholder: bio unit 4, next Friday

fields.label: What AI quizzes me from
fields.placeholder: my own notes, not the internet

fields.label: Quiz days before the test
fields.placeholder: 5 days out, 3 days out, 1 day out

fields.label: What happens to missed questions
fields.placeholder: flag them, re-test in two days

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: The exam is in four days and you have one hour tonight. Which move is the best use of it?

options.text: Reread the chapter until it feels familiar again
options.feedback: Familiar is the trap. Smooth rereading feels like knowing, but the test asks you to produce, not recognize.

options.text: Have AI write a clean summary of the unit and read it through a few times tonight
options.feedback: A better page to reread is still rereading. The summary is in front of you; on test day it will not be.

options.text: Quiz yourself from memory and flag what you miss
options.feedback: Right. Retrieval tonight strengthens the memory, and the flagged misses tell you exactly what to re-test before Friday.

options.text: Recopy your notes so they are neater for tomorrow
options.feedback: Copying is mostly hand work, not memory work. Your eyes never leave the original, so nothing gets retrieved.

lessons.title: Writing & research
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I keep my voice while using AI to write?
lessons.blurb: Keep the thinking and the sentences yours. Use AI as an editor and a research scout, not a ghostwriter.

resources.label: MLA Style Center: How to cite generative AI
Purdue OWL: Research and citation resources

steps.title: The essay you can’t remember writing
steps.scenario: You are cleaning out your school drive and you open an essay from last semester — one that got a decent grade. You read the first paragraph and feel nothing. You do not remember writing it, because mostly you did not: AI drafted it and you swapped a few words. Your name is at the top of a page you could not quote a single line from.
steps.prompt: The grade was fine. So what exactly went missing?

steps.title: Whose voice is it?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether the writing and thinking stay yours.

items.text: “Write my personal statement about my grandmother’s restaurant.”
“Here is my messy draft. Mark where my argument is unclear — do not rewrite my sentences.”
Asking AI to interview you with questions before you write a word
Pasting AI’s conclusion into your essay and changing three words

steps.reveal: The line is not “did AI touch it.” The line is who did the thinking and who chose the words. Feedback, questions, and gap-spotting keep you the writer. Generated sentences make you the editor of someone else’s essay.

steps.title: Repair the ghostwriter prompt
steps.weak: Write me a five-paragraph essay about social media for my English class.
fields: What I already wrote or believe
The job AI should do instead of writing
steps.strong: My claim: social media rewards outrage more than accuracy. Here is my rough draft: [paste draft]. Do not rewrite my sentences. Point out the two weakest spots in my argument, ask me three questions that would sharpen my claim, and list any statements I would need a real source for. Leave my wording and examples exactly as they are.

steps.title: Draft first, then borrow the editor
steps.body: The order matters. If you draft first — even a rough, awkward draft — AI can react to your ideas, and the voice stays yours. If AI drafts first, every revision happens inside its structure and phrasing, and your job quietly shrinks to approving someone else’s essay. For research it is the same rule: AI is a map, not a source. It can suggest what to look up, what the sides of a debate are, and what terms to search — but the sources you cite have to be ones you actually opened, because AI can describe papers and quotes that do not exist.
steps.mistake: Asking AI to write the first draft “just to get started,” then spending the night lightly editing its voice instead of writing in yours.
steps.good: Write the ugly first draft yourself, then ask AI for questions, weak spots, and claims to verify — and check every source it mentions before it goes near your bibliography.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is a paragraph I wrote: [paste your paragraph]. Do not rewrite it or suggest replacement sentences. Instead: 1) Tell me where my argument is weakest and why. 2) Ask me two questions that would make my point sharper. 3) List any claim in my paragraph that needs a real source, and tell me what kind of source would be strong. My wording stays mine.
steps.note: Run this on real homework or work writing. If the answers make you want to revise, you are using AI as an editor — the best kind of help.

fields.label: What I do before AI sees anything
fields.placeholder: my claim, my rough draft, my examples

fields.label: What AI is allowed to do
fields.placeholder: questions, weak spots, claims to verify

fields.label: What AI never writes for me
fields.placeholder: my sentences, personal stories, conclusions

fields.label: My source rule
fields.placeholder: only cite what I opened and read myself

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: The essay is due tomorrow and you are behind. Which use of AI keeps your voice?

options.text: Write a rough draft yourself, then ask AI for weak spots, questions, and claims to verify
options.feedback: Right. AI reacts to your ideas instead of replacing them, and the words stay yours.

options.text: Let AI write the first draft, then spend your time rewording it until the sentences feel more like yours
options.feedback: Rewording is still editing AI’s thinking. The structure, argument, and most of the phrasing stay borrowed.

options.text: Ask AI for finished paragraphs and list it as a source in your bibliography so everything stays honest
options.feedback: Citing it is honest, but the essay still is not your writing — and AI is not a reliable source of facts. MLA citation covers AI text you quote, not AI as evidence.

lessons.title: Coding & debugging
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI as a coding coach, not a crutch?
lessons.blurb: Use AI to write and fix code without losing the one skill that makes you a programmer: knowing why your code works.

resources.label: How to debug small programs (Eric Lippert)
How to ask a good programming question (Stack Overflow)

steps.title: The code that works until it doesn’t
steps.scenario: You ask AI for a function, paste in the 60 lines it gives you, and your project runs. A week later it crashes on one input — and you realize you cannot explain a single line of what you pasted.
steps.prompt: Whose code is it now? And who is going to fix it?

steps.title: Who is still the programmer?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it keeps you in charge of your program or quietly hands your understanding to the AI.

items.text: Pasting the exact error message and asking what it means before asking for a fix
Pasting in 60 lines you cannot read and shipping them because they run
Asking why the suggested fix works before you apply it
Letting AI rewrite the whole file when one function failed

steps.reveal: Running is not the same as understood. Every line you cannot explain is a line you cannot debug next week.

steps.title: Repair the bug report
steps.weak: my code doesn't work, fix it
fields: Exact error message or wrong output
steps.strong: I'm writing Python 3 for a class project. This function should return the average of a list, but on an empty list it crashes with: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero (line 4). Expected: return 0 for an empty list. Actual: crash. I tried wrapping it in try/except but that hid a different bug. Explain what is going wrong before suggesting any fix.

steps.title: Explain-first debugging
steps.body: AI is genuinely good at reading error messages, spotting typos, and drafting code. The danger is not that its code is bad — it is that accepting fixes you do not understand slowly turns your own project into a stranger’s codebase. The rule that protects you: explanation before fix. Make the AI teach you the bug, then make the change yourself.
steps.mistake: Pasting in a fix because the error went away, without knowing why it went away.
steps.good: Ask “what does this error mean, and which line causes it?” first. Apply the fix by typing it yourself, and only keep code you could explain to a classmate.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is my code: [paste code]. Here is the error or wrong output: [paste it]. Do NOT rewrite my code yet. First, explain in plain language what the error means. Second, point to the most likely line and explain why. Third, give me a hint so I can try the fix myself. Only show a full corrected version if I ask for it.
steps.note: This turns AI into a debugging tutor instead of a vending machine for code you cannot maintain.

fields.label: Reproduce it
fields.placeholder: smallest input that still breaks it

fields.label: What I tell the AI
fields.placeholder: language, exact error, expected vs. actual, what I tried

fields.label: Explain-first rule
fields.placeholder: AI explains the bug before I see any fix

fields.label: Ownership check
fields.placeholder: I type the fix and can explain every changed line

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: AI hands you a working fix for your broken function. What keeps you the programmer?

options.text: Apply the fix for now and keep moving — if something in that code breaks again later, that's a better moment to dig into what actually went wrong
options.feedback: Tempting, but the next bug probably won't look like this one — and by then the fix is weeks old and you can't explain the line that broke. Understanding is cheapest right now, while the error is fresh.

options.text: Ask the AI to explain the bug and the fix until you could explain it yourself, then apply it
options.feedback: Right. Explanation before fix keeps the program yours, even when AI helped write it.

options.text: Ask the AI to review the surrounding code too and clean it up while it's at it, since related bugs tend to hide near each other
options.feedback: Related bugs do cluster, but letting AI rework code you haven't understood yet just grows the pile of lines you can't explain. Understand this one fix first — expand the cleanup later if you choose to.

lessons.title: Creative work
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I keep originality and ownership with AI?
lessons.blurb: Use AI as a reaction partner for your stories, songs, and designs — without letting it sand off the weird parts that make the work yours.

resources.label: Ethan Mollick — Automating creativity (One Useful Thing)
Study: generative AI boosts individual creativity but reduces collective diversity (arXiv)

steps.title: The rewrite that erased you
steps.scenario: You paste a verse you wrote for a song — a little awkward, but it sounds like you — and ask AI to 'make it better.' It comes back smoother, cleaner, and somehow exactly like every other song lyric on the internet. Your weird line about the broken vending machine is gone.
steps.prompt: Smoother is not the same as better. What did you actually trade away?

steps.title: Keep the voice or lose it?
steps.prompt: You are working on a story, a song, a comic, a design — anything creative. Sort each move by what it does to your style.

items.text: Paste your draft and ask AI to rewrite the whole thing to sound better
Ask AI to list 15 directions the next scene could go, then write the one you pick yourself
Ask AI to point at the lines that feel flat or confusing — without rewriting them
Accept the AI version because it sounds more professional than yours
Show AI two of your old pieces first, so its feedback is about your voice, not a generic one

steps.reveal: The pattern: AI is safest as a reaction partner — generating options, spotting weak points, asking questions. The moment it writes the final words, the average voice starts replacing yours.

steps.title: Repair the flattening prompt
fields: What stays mine (the part AI must not rewrite)
The job AI does instead (critique, options, questions)
Style sample or reference (so feedback fits MY voice)
steps.strong: Here are two paragraphs I wrote before, so you know my voice: [paste samples]. Now here is my new story draft: [paste draft]. Do NOT rewrite it. Instead: (1) mark the three places where the pacing drags, (2) ask me two questions about what the main character wants, and (3) list five possible endings as one-line ideas only. I will do the writing.

steps.title: Why AI flattens, and what to do about it
steps.body: AI is trained to predict the most likely next words, so its default output drifts toward the most common version of everything — the average song, the average plot, the average poster. Research backs this up: AI help can make individual drafts score better while making everyone's work more alike. Your style lives in the un-average choices. So flip the roles: you make the choices, AI reacts to them — critiquing, questioning, and generating options you can reject.
steps.mistake: Treating the AI rewrite as the finish line because it reads smoother than your draft.
steps.good: Treat AI output as raw material and reactions. The final pass — word choice, weird details, what gets cut — is always yours.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I am working on a creative piece and I want feedback that protects my style, not a rewrite. First, here is a sample of my past work so you can hear my voice: [paste a short sample]. Now here is the current draft: [paste draft]. Do not rewrite any of it. Instead: 1) describe my voice in two sentences, 2) point at the three weakest spots and say WHY they are weak, 3) ask me three questions that would push the piece further, and 4) give me 8 one-line directions I could take next — including at least 2 strange ones.
steps.note: Works for stories, lyrics, scripts, art descriptions, even design briefs. Notice how different the session feels when AI is reacting to you instead of replacing you.

fields.label: My voice markers
fields.placeholder: short sentences, dark jokes, concrete details...

fields.label: Jobs AI is allowed to do
fields.placeholder: critique, options, questions, research

fields.label: Off limits for AI
fields.placeholder: final wording, the ending, my hooks

fields.label: My flattening check
fields.placeholder: could anyone have made this exact thing?

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: You wrote a song verse you mostly like. What is the best way to use AI on it?

options.text: Ask AI for a polished rewrite, then put it next to your draft and keep whichever version honestly reads better to you
options.feedback: The comparison feels fair, but smoother usually wins it — and smoother is the average voice. Polish is where flattening happens, even when you are the judge.

options.text: Ask AI to react: name the weakest line, ask questions, and list directions — then revise it yourself
options.feedback: Right. AI generates reactions and options; you make the creative choices that carry your style.

options.text: Have AI generate several alternate verses in roughly your style, and pick the one that feels closest to what you meant
options.feedback: Even 'in your style' drifts toward the average, and picking between AI verses is not the same as writing one. Choosing is not where your voice develops.

lessons.title: Personal productivity
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to plan without outsourcing my judgment?
lessons.blurb: Find the tasks where AI genuinely buys your time back — and spot the ones where it just gives you a shinier way to stall.

resources.label: Nielsen Norman Group: AI tools and productivity gains
Centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier (Ethan Mollick on the Harvard/BCG study)

steps.title: The 40-minute to-do list
steps.scenario: It is Sunday night. You ask AI to plan your week. Twenty minutes later you are still regenerating the plan, tweaking its wording, and asking for a “better” version. Your homework has not moved. You feel productive. You are not.
steps.prompt: Did the AI save you time tonight, or did it just make stalling feel like work?

steps.title: Time saved or time laundered?
steps.prompt: Sort each real-life move by whether it genuinely buys time back or quietly burns it.

items.text: Paste your syllabus and ask for every deadline as a dated checklist
Ask “plan my week” without telling it your classes, shifts, or deadlines
Draft a routine email (a reschedule request, a club reminder) that you edit and send
Regenerate the same answer five times hoping it magically gets better
Polish the wording of a to-do list instead of doing the first item on it

steps.reveal: AI saves time when it transforms input you already have — notes, a syllabus, a messy draft. It wastes time when you ask it to invent your life from nothing, or when fiddling with the output replaces doing the task.

steps.title: Repair the productivity prompt
steps.weak: Help me be more productive this week.
fields: What I actually have to get done
The real time slots I have free
What I will paste in (notes, syllabus, deadlines)
What a useful answer looks like
steps.strong: I have a biology test Friday, a 5-page history draft due Thursday, and work shifts Tuesday and Wednesday 4–8pm. I'm free Monday after 5, Thursday after 3, and Sunday afternoon. Here are my class notes and the essay prompt: [paste]. Make me a day-by-day plan that fits those slots, puts the hardest work earliest, and flags anything that won't fit so I can cut or ask for an extension.

steps.title: The honest math of saved time
steps.body: AI saves time on tasks with three properties: you can hand it the real input, you can judge the output fast, and the output is a draft you finish — not a decision it makes for you. Summarizing your own notes, turning a syllabus into deadlines, and first drafts of routine messages all pass. Vague life-planning, endless regeneration, and outsourcing the thinking you needed to practice all fail — they cost time now or cost you more later when the “learning” didn't happen.
steps.mistake: Counting the time AI spends typing as time you saved, while ignoring the 25 minutes you spent prompting, re-prompting, and reformatting.
steps.good: Before using AI on a task, estimate doing it yourself. If prompting plus checking is not clearly faster — or if the struggle was the point, like studying — just do the task.

steps.title: Run a time audit on your real week
steps.prompt: Here are three tasks eating my time this week: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3]. For each one, tell me honestly: (1) could AI realistically save time, or would it just add a step? (2) what exact input would I have to give you for the output to be useful? (3) which part should I still do myself — because of accuracy, privacy, or because it's the part I need to learn? Be blunt. If AI is the slower option for one of these, say so.
steps.note: Run this in any chatbot with your actual tasks. The most useful answer is often the one telling you not to use AI.

fields.label: Recurring task AI genuinely speeds up
fields.placeholder: syllabus to deadline list, first-draft emails

fields.label: Input I must paste in first
fields.placeholder: my notes, the syllabus, my real schedule

fields.label: My time box
fields.placeholder: if prompting passes 10 minutes, do it myself

fields.label: Task I keep AI out of
fields.placeholder: studying for tests, messages to friends

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which daily task is AI most likely to genuinely save you time on?

options.text: Turning a syllabus you paste in into a dated deadline checklist you double-check
options.feedback: Right. Real input, fast-to-verify output, and you stay the editor — that is the sweet spot.

options.text: Asking it to plan your week before giving it your classes, shifts, or deadlines, figuring you can correct the details once you see a draft
options.feedback: Without your real constraints, it can only produce a generic plan — you spend the saved time fixing it.

options.text: Having it condense your notes before a test so you can study from the shorter version instead of working back through everything
options.feedback: That feels fast but offloads the exact struggle that makes the material stick. The cost shows up on test day.

lessons.title: Business & workflows
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a messy task into an AI-assisted workflow?
lessons.blurb: Use AI at work for real tasks — emails, notes, summaries — without leaking private data or sending unchecked output.

resources.label: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
OECD AI Principles

steps.title: The intern with no judgment
steps.scenario: A teammate pastes a customer’s complaint — name, account number, full history — into a free chatbot and asks for a reply. The draft sounds professional, so they hit send. Two risks just happened, and neither one was the writing.
steps.prompt: Can you name both risks before this lesson does?

steps.title: Safe task or new risk?
steps.prompt: Real workplace moves. Sort each one by whether it is a careful use of AI or whether it just created a new risk.

items.text: Drafting a routine status-update email, then reading and editing it before sending
Pasting a customer’s name, account number, and complaint into a public chatbot
Turning your own messy meeting notes into action items you double-check
Letting AI auto-send replies to clients with no one reading them first
Uploading a confidential contract to a free tool to summarize the terms
Asking AI to explain a spreadsheet formula a coworker built

steps.reveal: Every risky one breaks the same two rules: private data went in, or unchecked output went out. The careful ones keep both doors guarded.

steps.title: Build the safe email workflow
steps.goal: Your team gets the same kinds of customer-question emails every week. Use AI to answer them faster — without leaking data or sending a mistake.
correct: Strip names, account numbers, and private details from the email
Ask AI to draft a reply in the team’s tone
Check the draft for wrong promises or made-up policy
Add the real customer details back yourself
A human approves before anything is sent
steps.note: Notice the shape: redact before AI sees it, verify before anyone else sees it. That shape works for almost any team task.

steps.title: Two doors, two guards
steps.body: Team AI risk is not really about the AI. It is about two doors: what goes IN (customer data, contracts, anything confidential) and what goes OUT (replies, summaries, decisions that reach real people). A safe workflow guards both — redact the input, and put a named human between the output and the world. Speed is fine; skipping the check is what causes the incident.
steps.mistake: Treating a polished draft as a finished one. Confident-sounding output is exactly when teams stop reading carefully.
steps.good: Decide before you start: what gets redacted, who checks the output, and whose name is on the send button.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I want to use AI for this work task: [describe the task]. Before I start, help me risk-check it. 1) List what information I would be sharing and flag anything private, confidential, or owned by a customer. 2) Tell me who would see the output and what happens if it is wrong. 3) Tell me where the human review step should go. Then show me a redacted version of my input that is still useful.
steps.note: Run this on a real task — a school club email, a part-time job message, a group project doc. The two-door check works at any scale.

fields.label: Repeated work task
fields.placeholder: answer customer emails, summarize meetings

fields.label: What never goes in
fields.placeholder: names, account numbers, confidential files

fields.label: Output check
fields.placeholder: wrong promises, made-up policy, off tone

fields.label: Who approves before send
fields.placeholder: me, my manager, the account owner

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: A teammate wants AI to draft replies to customer complaints. What makes the plan safe?

options.text: Switch to a paid business tool with a data agreement, since the company has presumably vetted how it handles customer information
options.feedback: A vetted tool helps with the input side, maybe — but it does nothing about unreviewed replies going out. The tool choice cannot replace guarding both doors.

options.text: Redact private details going in, and have a person review every reply going out
options.feedback: Right. Guard both doors: what the AI sees, and what reaches the customer.

options.text: Start with low-stakes complaints, and once the drafts have looked solid for a few weeks, let it handle most replies on its own
options.feedback: A trial period feels careful, but past drafts being good does not make the next one safe. The review step is what catches the bad one — removing it removes the safety.

lessons.title: Teachers & classrooms
lessons.coreQuestion: How can a teacher use AI without replacing thinking?
lessons.blurb: AI can save a teacher hours — and quietly wreck an assignment. Learn where it helps, why detectors fail, and how to design work where the learning stays visible.

resources.label: UNESCO: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
Common Sense Media: AI product reviews for schools and families

steps.title: Two teachers, same tool
steps.scenario: One teacher uses AI to write three versions of the same worked example — one for students who missed last week, one on grade level, one for students who are ahead. Another teacher runs every essay through an AI detector and fails anyone who scores above 60%. Same technology, very different judgment.
steps.prompt: Which classroom would you rather be in — and what exactly is the second teacher getting wrong?

steps.title: Good use or redesign needed?
steps.prompt: Sort each classroom move: is the teacher using AI well, or is this a move that needs a redesign or a stop?

items.text: Drafting the same worked example at three reading levels, then checking each for errors
Failing a student because an AI detector flagged their essay
Generating practice quiz questions, then verifying every answer against the textbook
Pasting a student's grades and learning-plan details into a public chatbot
Asking AI for five ways students might misunderstand tomorrow's topic
Letting AI write report-card comments and sending them without reading

steps.reveal: The pattern: AI is great for drafts, variations, and anticipating confusion — things the teacher checks before students see them. It fails when it becomes the judge of a student or a leak of their private data. Detectors are unreliable and flag innocent work, especially from students writing in a second language.

steps.title: Redesign the assignment, not the surveillance
steps.goal: An essay assignment is easy to complete with AI and learn nothing. Redesign it so the learning stays visible — without relying on detectors.
correct: Name the skill the assignment actually measures
Set a clear AI-use rule students can actually follow
Require process evidence: outline, draft, and what changed
Add an in-class or oral component tied to their own draft
Grade the thinking and revisions, not just the polished page
steps.note: Each step builds on the last: you cannot write a fair AI rule until you know what skill you are measuring, and process evidence only means something if the grade actually looks at it. Detectors guess; this design makes the learning observable.

steps.title: Design beats detection
steps.body: Teachers who use AI well treat it like a tireless assistant for visible work — differentiated examples, quiz drafts, anticipated misconceptions — and keep two things firmly human: judging students and protecting their data. And the answer to misuse is not a detector arms race. It is assignments where the thinking has to show up — drafts, revisions, in-class explanations — so using AI as a shortcut stops paying off.
steps.mistake: Treating an AI detector score as proof. Detectors misfire often enough that they have falsely accused real students, and they disproportionately flag non-native English writers.
steps.good: If work seems off, talk to the student about their own draft. Someone who wrote it can explain it; that conversation is fairer and more accurate than any score.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I teach [subject] to [grade level]. Here is an assignment: [paste assignment]. First, show me the three easiest ways a student could complete it with AI while learning nothing. Then suggest a redesign that keeps the learning visible — process evidence, in-class components, or oral checks — and a one-sentence AI-use rule I could give students.
steps.note: This works for teachers, tutors, club leaders — anyone who assigns work. You are using AI to red-team the assignment before students do.

fields.label: Skill it really measures
fields.placeholder: argument building, problem solving, source analysis

fields.label: AI-use rule in one sentence
fields.placeholder: AI for brainstorming only; every draft is yours

fields.label: Process evidence required
fields.placeholder: outline, messy draft, note on what changed

fields.label: In-person check
fields.placeholder: 2-minute explanation of your own argument

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: A teacher suspects an essay was AI-written. What is the strongest move?

options.text: Compare the essay with the student's earlier work, and if the style seems different, use an AI detector score to back up that impression
options.feedback: It sounds careful, but it stacks two guesses. Style shifts for honest reasons — a new topic, more revision, growth — and detectors misfire often, especially on students writing in a second language. A hunch plus a shaky score is still not evidence.

options.text: Ask the student to walk through their draft and explain their own argument
options.feedback: Right. A student who did the thinking can show the thinking. That conversation is fairer and more accurate than any detector — and better assignment design makes it routine, not an accusation.

options.text: Give this essay the benefit of the doubt, since nothing can be proven, and tighten the assignment's AI rules going forward
options.feedback: Better rules for next time are genuinely useful — but "nothing can be proven" gives up too early. You can learn a lot right now by having the student talk through their own draft. Skipping that skips the fairest evidence available.

lessons.title: From prompt to workflow
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I chain prompts into a repeatable workflow?
lessons.blurb: Turn a repeated AI task into a small system with inputs, checks, saved output, and a human approval point.

steps.title: The repeated-task problem
steps.scenario: You keep asking AI to help with the same kind of task: summarize notes, make a study plan, check a draft, or turn ideas into a project outline. Each time, you rewrite the prompt from scratch.
steps.prompt: A workflow is how you stop starting over. It turns one useful prompt into a repeatable path.

steps.title: Sort the pieces
steps.prompt: Decide whether each piece is a one-off prompt, a workflow step, or unsafe automation.

items.text: “Explain this paragraph.”
Collect the input before asking AI to transform it.
Send the AI answer automatically without anyone checking it.
Compare the output against a rubric before saving it.

steps.reveal: A workflow is not more magic. It is a safer sequence of small steps.

steps.title: Build the safe order
steps.goal: Create a repeatable workflow for turning messy class notes into a useful study guide.
correct: Collect the notes and goal
Ask AI for a first draft
Check facts and missing parts
Revise the prompt or output
Save the final study guide
Decide what still needs human review
steps.note: The order matters because AI output should be inspected before it becomes something you rely on.

steps.title: What changed?
steps.body: A prompt asks for one answer. A workflow defines the input, the AI job, the check, the saved artifact, and the human approval point. That is how you begin building with AI instead of only chatting with it.
steps.mistake: Skipping the check step because the AI answer sounds polished.
steps.good: Make the check part of the workflow so quality is not optional.

fields.label: AI instruction
fields.placeholder: What the AI should do

fields.label: Verification check

steps.question: Which version is a real workflow?

options.text: Ask AI to “make it better” until it sounds good
options.feedback: That is still a loose conversation, not a repeatable path.

options.text: Input → AI draft → check → revise → save → human approval
options.feedback: Right. The workflow includes checks and a decision point.

options.text: Let AI receive, rewrite, and send everything automatically
options.feedback: That removes the safety and judgment steps.

lessons.title: Designing AI tools
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I design a small AI-powered tool?
lessons.blurb: Your best prompt works because of context in your head. A tool packs that context into the instructions, so it works for someone who was never in your chat.

resources.label: Anthropic: Prompt engineering overview
Google People + AI Guidebook — designing AI tools people can use

steps.title: The prompt that only works for you
steps.scenario: You built a prompt that turns your club's event details into a clean announcement post. It works every time. A friend asks for it, pastes it into a fresh chat, and gets junk: wrong tone, missing details, made-up dates.
steps.prompt: Nothing broke. The prompt was leaning on context that lived in your head and your chat history. A tool cannot lean on that.

steps.title: Shareable or stuck in your head?
steps.prompt: You are packaging your announcement prompt for the rest of the club. Sort each line: would it survive in a stranger's fresh chat, or does it secretly depend on you?

items.text: “Write it like we did last time.”
“Using only the event details pasted below, write a 3-sentence announcement.”
“Use the usual tone.”
“If the date, time, or location is missing, ask for it instead of guessing.”
“You know what our advisor wants.”

steps.reveal: “Last time,” “the usual,” and “you know” are pointers to context only you have. A tool spells that context out so a fresh chat — and a new user — gets the same result you do.

steps.title: Repair it into a tool
steps.weak: Make an announcement for the club thing. You know the vibe.
fields: Input slots the user fills in, like [EVENT NAME] and [DATE]
Rule for missing or bad input
steps.strong: You write event announcements for a high-school robotics club. Job: turn raw event details into one post. Inputs the user will paste: [EVENT NAME], [DATE & TIME], [LOCATION], [ONE THING THAT MAKES IT FUN]. Output: exactly 3 sentences, friendly but not slangy, ending with where to sign up. If any input slot is empty or contradictory, list what is missing and stop — do not invent details.

steps.title: A tool is a prompt with the context packed in
steps.body: A personal prompt borrows from your memory and your chat history. A tool carries everything with it: a one-line job, labeled input slots, a fixed output format, and a rule for bad input. That last one matters most — other people will paste in messy, incomplete stuff you never would, and a tool that quietly invents a date is worse than no tool.
steps.mistake: Shipping the prompt exactly as you use it, then blaming the user when it fails.
steps.good: Test it cold: open a blank chat, or hand it to one person who was not there, and watch where it breaks before you share it widely.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I have a prompt that works well for me, and I want to turn it into a tool other people can use: [paste your prompt]. First, interview me — ask about any context I am assuming that a stranger would not have. Then rewrite it as a reusable tool with: a one-line job description, labeled input slots in [BRACKETS], a fixed output format, and a rule for what to do when an input is missing or contradictory.
steps.note: Run this on a prompt you actually reuse. The interview step usually surfaces two or three assumptions you did not know you were making.

fields.label: One job
fields.placeholder: what this tool does, in one sentence

fields.label: Input slots
fields.placeholder: [NOTES], [AUDIENCE], [DEADLINE]

fields.label: Output format
fields.placeholder: length, tone, structure

fields.label: Bad-input rule
fields.placeholder: ask, don't guess; list what's missing

fields.label: Cold test
fields.placeholder: who tried it in a fresh chat, and what broke

steps.title: Exit check
steps.question: Your prompt works great for you. What actually turns it into a tool someone else can use?

options.text: Add more detail and examples until the prompt feels thorough enough that it should mostly work for other people, even if you cannot predict exactly what they will paste in
options.feedback: Length alone is not the fix. A very detailed prompt can still say “the usual tone” and lean on context only you have — what matters is what the detail covers, not how much there is.

options.text: Send along your whole chat transcript with the prompt, since seeing how the conversation actually went gives them most of the context they would otherwise be missing
options.feedback: Tempting, but their inputs will differ from yours, and your transcript may carry private details. Pack the context into the instructions instead, so it travels with the tool.

options.text: Move the hidden context into the prompt itself: one job, labeled input slots, a fixed format, and a rule for missing input — then test it in a fresh chat
options.feedback: Right. A tool carries its context with it, and the cold test proves it.

lessons.title: Intro to agents
lessons.coreQuestion: What is an agent, and what does it need to act safely?
lessons.blurb: A chatbot answers you. An agent takes steps and uses tools on your behalf. Learn to tell them apart, and to decide when handing over actions is worth it.

resources.label: Anthropic: Building effective agents

steps.title: It answered. Then it acted.
steps.scenario: You ask a chatbot how to compare three laptops, and it explains how. A friend shows you something different: they type a budget, and the AI searches stores, reads reviews, builds a comparison table, and drafts an email asking a seller about warranty — all on its own.
steps.prompt: Same kind of model underneath. So what actually changed?

steps.title: Chatbot or agent?
steps.prompt: Sort each behavior. A chatbot responds inside the conversation. An agent works toward a goal by taking steps and using tools.

items.text: Explains the difference between two history essay thesis statements you pasted in
Searches three sites, compares ticket prices, and reports back with the cheapest option
Rewrites your club announcement when you ask for a friendlier tone
Checks your calendar, finds a free slot for the study group, and drafts the invite

steps.reveal: The dividing line is not how smart the answer sounds. It is whether the AI only replies, or whether it takes actions — searching, reading files, drafting, scheduling — across multiple steps toward your goal.

steps.title: Give it only the tools it needs
steps.goal: An agent that checks your school email each morning, drafts replies to routine club-scheduling questions, and flags anything important for you to handle yourself.

tools.name: Save replies as drafts for your review
Send emails without showing you first

steps.title: An agent is a chatbot with hands
steps.body: An agent is a model plus three things: a goal it keeps working toward, tools it can use (search, files, email, calendar), and a loop where it checks its own progress and tries the next step. That is powerful — and it means mistakes are no longer just wrong sentences. They can be wrong actions. So the question shifts from “is this answer right?” to “what is this allowed to do, and where do I approve before anything real happens?”
steps.mistake: Wanting an agent because it sounds advanced, then giving it broad access “to be safe.”
steps.good: Want an agent for repetitive multi-step tasks you can describe clearly. Give it the minimum tools, keep actions reversible (drafts, not sends), and keep an approval point where you decide.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I am learning what AI agents are. Here is a task I do repeatedly: [describe your task]. Pretend you are an agent assigned this task. List: (1) the steps you would take in order, (2) the tools or access you would need for each step, (3) the step where a mistake would be hardest to undo, and (4) where a human approval checkpoint should go. Then tell me honestly whether this task even needs an agent, or whether a regular chat prompt would do.
steps.note: You are not building an agent yet — you are learning to read one like a plan, which is exactly the skill you need before you trust one.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the core difference between an agent and a chatbot?

options.text: An agent usually runs on a bigger, more capable model, which is what lets it handle harder tasks than an ordinary chatbot could
options.feedback: Often the model is the same one. The difference is what it is allowed and set up to do, not raw intelligence.

options.text: An agent takes multi-step actions with tools toward a goal, while a chatbot only responds in the conversation
options.feedback: Right. Goal, tools, and a step-by-step loop — which is also why approval points matter more.

options.text: Agents tend to end up more accurate, since checking their own work at each step lets them catch mistakes a one-shot chatbot would miss
options.feedback: Agents can compound errors across steps. More autonomy means more places to go wrong, not fewer.

lessons.title: Voice agents & interfaces
lessons.coreQuestion: What changes when the interface is voice?
lessons.blurb: Voice makes AI feel more human and hides more errors. Learn when speaking beats typing, what gets misheard, and why a talking agent needs a confirm step before it acts.

resources.label: Mozilla Common Voice — why voice AI needs diverse accents and languages
FTC alert: scammers use AI voice cloning in family-emergency schemes

steps.title: The agent that heard you wrong
steps.scenario: You tell a voice assistant, “Text Sam I can’t make it.” It cheerfully replies, “Okay, texting Pam: I can make it.” With typing, you would have seen the mistake before hitting send. With voice, the error happened in the air, and the agent was already acting on it.
steps.prompt: What did you lose when the keyboard and screen went away — and what did you gain?

steps.title: Voice or screen?
steps.prompt: Sort each task by whether voice plays to its strengths or whether you are better off typing and reading.

items.text: Practicing interview answers or a language conversation out loud
Comparing five options with prices, dates, and trade-offs
Asking quick questions while your hands are busy cooking or walking
Giving an exact ID number, address, or unusual name that must be letter-perfect

steps.reveal: Voice is great for hands-free, back-and-forth, and practice. Screens win when you need to skim, compare, or be exact — spoken words vanish, and you cannot reread them.

steps.title: Design a phone-line voice agent
steps.goal: Build a voice agent that answers your club’s phone line, tells callers the next meeting time, and takes a message for a human to read later.

tools.name: Read-only access to the club calendar
A message log a human reviews
Permission to edit or cancel calendar events
Access to every member’s private contact list
Ability to take payments over the phone

steps.title: What actually changes with voice
steps.body: The model behind a voice agent is mostly the same — what changes is the interface. Speech-to-text can mishear you, and you may never see the wrong transcript. Spoken answers are linear, so you cannot skim or double-check mid-sentence. And because a voice sounds human, people trust it faster — which is exactly why voice scams using cloned voices work. So a voice agent that acts on what it hears needs one extra habit: say back what it understood before it does anything.
steps.mistake: Letting a voice agent send, book, or buy straight from what it heard, because the conversation felt natural.
steps.good: Give voice agents read-only powers by default, and require a spoken confirmation — “You want me to text Sam, correct?” — before any action.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I want to use a voice interface with AI for this task: [describe your task]. Tell me: 1) whether voice or typing fits this task better and why, 2) what is likely to be misheard or lost when it is spoken instead of written (names, numbers, homophones, accents), and 3) one confirmation step I should require before the AI acts on anything I say out loud.
steps.note: If your chatbot has a voice mode, try the same question twice — once typed, once spoken — and compare what got lost.
