steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the biggest new risk when an AI agent listens and acts instead of showing you text?

options.text: Voice systems tend to run on smaller, faster models so they can respond in real time, which means the reasoning behind the answers is probably weaker than what you would get by typing
options.feedback: Reasonable guess, but the model behind a voice agent is usually the same one you would type to. The risk lives in the interface — hearing you and speaking back — not in the intelligence behind it.

options.text: A mishearing can silently become a wrong action, so the agent should confirm before it acts
options.feedback: Right. Without a screen, you may never see the wrong transcript. A say-it-back confirmation step catches the error before it becomes an action.

options.text: Spoken conversations tend to be shorter and less detailed than typed ones, so the agent is working from less context and gives you a shallower answer than it could
options.feedback: People do often say less than they would type, but that mostly costs you detail, not safety. The new risk is that you never see what the agent thought you said before it acts on it.

lessons.title: Evaluation & testing
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I know my AI thing actually works before I share it?
lessons.blurb: One great demo is not proof. Build a tiny test set, decide what “good” means before you look, and earn the right to hit share.

resources.label: Anthropic: Create strong empirical evaluations
Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals

steps.title: It worked once. Now what?
steps.scenario: You built a study-guide prompt for your bio class. You ran it on your own notes, the output looked amazing, and you are about to send it to the group chat. But you tested it on one input — the exact notes you built it around.
steps.prompt: What happens when someone pastes in messy notes, a different subject, or half a chapter?

steps.title: Real test or false confidence?
steps.prompt: You want evidence your AI thing works, not just a good feeling. Sort each move.

items.text: It produced one great output on the example I built it with
Run it on five real inputs from classmates, including one messy one
Write down what a good output must include before reading any output
Ask the AI to rate its own answer out of 10
Try an input where the right behavior is to say “I can’t do this”
The output sounds confident and is nicely formatted

steps.reveal: A real test uses inputs you did not design around, a definition of “good” you wrote in advance, and at least one case built to break it. Polish, confidence, and self-grading prove nothing.

steps.title: Build the test routine
steps.goal: Test your study-guide prompt before sharing it with the group chat.
correct: Write down what a good output must include
Collect five real inputs, including a messy one and a breaker
Run the prompt on every input
Score each output against your checklist
Fix the worst failure and re-run the tests
Decide if it is good enough to share
steps.note: The checklist comes first on purpose. If you read outputs before defining “good,” a fluent answer will talk you into lowering the bar.

steps.title: A demo is not evidence
steps.body: One great output is a demo: it shows your thing CAN work. Evaluation shows it RELIABLY works — across inputs you did not handpick, judged against criteria you set before looking. Even five honest test cases beat fifty lucky demos, because they tell you where it breaks and whether the failures are ones you can live with.
steps.mistake: Testing only on friendly inputs, then being surprised when a real user’s messy, weird, or off-topic input embarrasses you.
steps.good: Include at least one hard case and one case where the right answer is “refuse or admit uncertainty.” How it fails matters as much as how it succeeds.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I built this AI prompt/tool: [paste your prompt and what it is supposed to do]. Help me test it before I share it. 1) Generate five realistic test inputs: two normal, two messy or hard, and one designed to make it fail gracefully. 2) Give me a four-point checklist for judging each output, written so a stranger could apply it. Do NOT run the prompt or grade the outputs for me — I will run the tests and judge them myself.
steps.note: AI is great at inventing test cases and checklists. The judging stays with you — that is the part that keeps the test honest.

fields.placeholder: cover key terms, cite the notes, no invented facts

fields.label: Test inputs
fields.placeholder: 2 normal, 2 messy, 1 designed to break it

steps.title: Exit check
steps.question: You ran your AI tool once and the output looked great. What does that actually tell you?

options.text: It is probably fine to share — the input was realistic, and if a classmate hits a problem they can tell you and you can patch it then
options.feedback: One polished output on a friendly input is a demo, not evidence. Fix-it-later means the first messy real input embarrasses you in the group chat instead of in private testing.

options.text: It CAN work — now test it on inputs you did not design it around, including ones meant to break it
options.feedback: Right. Define “good” first, test on varied real inputs, and check how it fails before you share.

options.text: Honestly not much either way — outputs vary so much between runs that even a small test set mostly measures luck, so more testing will not settle it
options.feedback: Single outputs do vary, but patterns across even five honest test cases are real evidence — that is exactly why you run more than one case instead of giving up on testing.

lessons.title: Build a capstone
lessons.coreQuestion: Can I combine everything into one real project?
lessons.blurb: Take one real project from idea to finished — with AI as your partner and your judgment running the whole thing.

resources.label: What is project-based learning? (PBLWorks / Buck Institute)
MIT RAISE — free AI literacy resources

steps.title: One project, every skill
steps.scenario: You have practiced prompting, verifying, spotting bias, building workflows, and knowing when to skip AI. A capstone is where it all meets: one real thing — a study guide for your AP Bio class, a fundraiser plan for your club, a FAQ page for the place you volunteer — built with AI helping and you in charge.
steps.prompt: What is one real thing you could finish in a week or two that someone besides you would actually use?

steps.title: Is this capstone ready to build?
steps.prompt: A good capstone is specific, finishable, and stays yours. Sort each project plan.

items.text: A one-page study guide for next month's chemistry final, checked against the textbook
"An app that helps everyone learn everything better"
Paste the assignment into AI, submit whatever comes out, done in ten minutes
A volunteer-shift FAQ for the food bank, with answers verified by the coordinator
A project where you cannot say which parts AI did and which parts you did

steps.reveal: Ready means: a real audience, a scope you can finish, facts you can verify, and a clear line between AI's work and yours.

steps.title: Build the capstone path
steps.goal: Take a real project — say, a study guide your whole class will use — from idea to something you can stand behind.
correct: Define the project, the audience, and what 'done' looks like
Split it into pieces and decide where AI helps and where it should not
Draft with AI one piece at a time, with your own input first
Verify every fact and claim against a source you can open
Test it on a real person and fix what confuses them
Ship it, and be ready to explain what you did versus what AI did
steps.note: Notice where verification sits: before anyone else relies on your work, not after. This is every earlier lesson stacked into one path.

steps.title: A capstone proves judgment, not just output
steps.body: Anyone can generate pages of AI text. A capstone shows you can scope a real problem, direct AI where it helps, catch where it is wrong, and ship something a real person can use. The finished project matters, but the part you keep is the proof that you can run the whole loop yourself.
steps.mistake: Treating the capstone as one giant prompt: paste the goal, take the output, call it done. You end up with something polished that you cannot defend, because you never checked it and none of the decisions were yours.
steps.good: Stay the project lead. AI drafts pieces, you set the scope, verify the facts, test with a real user, and make every call about what ships.

steps.title: Plan your capstone for real
steps.prompt: I want to build a capstone project: [describe your project and who it is for]. Help me plan it, but do not do it for me. 1) Suggest a scope I can finish in two weeks. 2) Break it into 4-6 pieces, and for each piece say whether AI drafting helps or whether I should do it myself, and why. 3) List the claims or facts I will need to verify and where I could check them. 4) Tell me what 'done' should look like and one way to test it with a real person.
steps.note: Run this in any chatbot. If the plan it gives you has no verification step or no human test, that is your cue to add them — the model will not insist on them, but you should.

steps.title: Exit check
steps.question: What makes a capstone genuinely yours, even with AI helping?

options.text: You did most of the writing yourself and only leaned on AI for smaller things, like tightening wording or cleaning up structure
options.feedback: How much AI you used is not the test. You could write most of it yourself and still not own it, or let AI draft a lot and own all of it. What matters is who made the calls — and whether you can defend them.

options.text: You set the scope, verified the facts, made the decisions, and can explain what AI did versus what you did
options.feedback: Right. Ownership is about judgment and accountability — you ran the project, AI drafted pieces, and you can defend every part.

options.text: You edited the final version enough that it reads in your own voice and reflects how you would naturally explain things
options.feedback: Sounding like you is not the same as being yours. A smooth edit can sit on top of facts you never checked and decisions you never made. If you cannot explain why each part is there, the voice does not save it.
